claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PtenKO neurons have large soma size but correct positioning.

claims.claim: Recorded neurons displayed increased membrane capacitance in all experimental conditions.
claims.source: Consistent with the changes in soma size (Figure 1c and e), recorded neurons displayed increased membrane capacitance in all experimental conditions (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: Neurons expressing the MTORS2215Y variant had a larger capacitance increase than those expressing the RhebY35L variant.
claims.source: Neurons expressing the MTORS2215Y variant had a larger capacitance increase than those expressing the RhebY35L variant.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: PtenKO and Tsc1KO neurons had similar increases in capacitance that were both larger than that of the Depdc5KO neurons.
claims.source: PtenKO and Tsc1KO neurons had similar increases in capacitance that were both larger than that of the Depdc5KO neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: All neurons across the experimental conditions had increased resting membrane conductance in a pattern that followed that of the capacitance.
claims.source: All neurons across the experimental conditions also had increased resting membrane conductance in a pattern that followed that of the capacitance (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and Tsc1KO expression led to depolarized resting membrane potential (RMP).
claims.source: However, while RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and Tsc1KO expression led to depolarized resting membrane potential (RMP), Depdc5KO and PtenKO expression did not significantly affect the RMP (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: Depdc5KO and PtenKO expression did not significantly affect the RMP.
claims.source: However, while RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and Tsc1KO expression led to depolarized resting membrane potential (RMP), Depdc5KO and PtenKO expression did not significantly affect the RMP (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: For all experimental conditions, neurons fired fewer APs for current injections above 100 pA compared to the respective control neurons.
claims.source: For all experimental conditions, neurons fired fewer APs for current injections above 100 pA compared to the respective control neurons (Figure 2e and f, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2e and f.

claims.claim: The decrease in intrinsic excitability is reflected in the increased rheobase in all experimental conditions.
claims.source: This decrease in intrinsic excitability is reflected in the increased rheobase (i.e. the minimum current required to induce an AP) in all experimental conditions, with the MTORS2215Y and RhebY35L conditions leading to the largest rheobase increases (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2g.

claims.claim: The MTORS2215Y and RhebY35L conditions led to the largest rheobase increases.
claims.source: This decrease in intrinsic excitability is reflected in the increased rheobase (i.e. the minimum current required to induce an AP) in all experimental conditions, with the MTORS2215Y and RhebY35L conditions leading to the largest rheobase increases (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2g.

claims.claim: RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and Tsc1KO neurons display a decreased ability to generate APs upon depolarization despite having depolarized RMPs.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings indicate that RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and Tsc1KO neurons display a decreased ability to generate APs upon depolarization despite having depolarized RMPs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of depolarized RMP and increased rheobase in these conditions.

claims.claim: An initial spike doublet was observed in control neurons, consistent with the expected firing pattern for layer 2/3 mPFC pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: However, while an initial spike doublet was observed in control neurons, consistent with the expected firing pattern for layer 2/3 mPFC pyramidal neurons (Kroon et al., 2019), this was absent in all the experimental conditions except for the PtenKO condition (Figure 2e).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2e and citation to Kroon et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The initial spike doublet was absent in all the experimental conditions except for the PtenKO condition.
claims.source: However, while an initial spike doublet was observed in control neurons, consistent with the expected firing pattern for layer 2/3 mPFC pyramidal neurons (Kroon et al., 2019), this was absent in all the experimental conditions except for the PtenKO condition (Figure 2e).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, and Tsc1KO neurons had significantly increased first ISI compared to control neurons.
claims.source: Further quantification of the first interspike interval (first ISI; interval between the first and second AP) revealed significantly increased first ISI in RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, and Tsc1KO neurons, but not in PtenKO neurons, compared to control neurons (Figure 2h, Figure 2—figure supplement 1e, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2h.

claims.claim: PtenKO neurons did not have significantly increased first ISI compared to control neurons.
claims.source: Further quantification of the first interspike interval (first ISI; interval between the first and second AP) revealed significantly increased first ISI in RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, and Tsc1KO neurons, but not in PtenKO neurons, compared to control neurons (Figure 2h, Figure 2—figure supplement 1e, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2h.

claims.claim: No differences in the AP threshold were observed across the conditions.
claims.source: No differences in the AP threshold were observed across the conditions (Figure 2i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1f, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2i.

claims.claim: The AP peak amplitude was decreased in the MTORS2215Y and Tsc1KO conditions.
claims.source: The AP peak amplitude was decreased in the MTORS2215Y and Tsc1KO conditions (Figure 2j, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g, Figure 2—source data 1), while the AP half-width was decreased in the RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and PtenKO conditions (Figure 2k, Figure 2—figure supplement 1h, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2j.

claims.claim: The AP half-width was decreased in the RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and PtenKO conditions.
claims.source: The AP peak amplitude was decreased in the MTORS2215Y and Tsc1KO conditions (Figure 2j, Figure 2—figure supplement 1g, Figure 2—source data 1), while the AP half-width was decreased in the RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and PtenKO conditions (Figure 2k, Figure 2—figure supplement 1h, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2k.

claims.claim: Various genetic conditions that activate the mTORC1 pathway universally lead to decreased depolarization-induced excitability in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings show that various genetic conditions that activate the mTORC1 pathway universally lead to decreased depolarization-induced excitability in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, with gene-dependent changes in RMP and several AP properties.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the combined electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Neurons expressing RhebS16H display abnormal expression of HCN4 channels.
claims.source: We recently reported that neurons expressing RhebS16H, an mTORC1-activating variant of Rheb, display abnormal expression of HCN4 channels (Hsieh et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hsieh et al., 2020 and Nguyen et al., 2022.

claims.claim: HCN4 channels give rise to a hyperpolarization-activated cation current (Ih) that is normally absent in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: These channels give rise to a hyperpolarization-activated cation current (Ih) that is normally absent in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons (Hsieh et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hsieh et al., 2020 and Nguyen et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The aberrant Ih preceded seizure onset and was detected by P8-12 in mice.
claims.source: The aberrant Ih, which has implications for neuronal excitability, preceded seizure onset and was detected by P8-12 in mice (Hsieh et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hsieh et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment starting at P1 prevented the aberrant HCN4 channel expression.
claims.source: Rapamycin treatment starting at P1 and expression of constitutive active 4E-BP1, a translational repressor downstream of mTORC1, prevented and alleviated the aberrant HCN4 channel expression, respectively (Hsieh et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hsieh et al., 2020 and Nguyen et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Expression of constitutive active 4E-BP1 alleviated the aberrant HCN4 channel expression.
claims.source: Rapamycin treatment starting at P1 and expression of constitutive active 4E-BP1, a translational repressor downstream of mTORC1, prevented and alleviated the aberrant HCN4 channel expression, respectively (Hsieh et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hsieh et al., 2020 and Nguyen et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The abnormal HCN4 channel expression is mTORC1-dependent.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the abnormal HCN4 channel expression is mTORC1-dependent.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the effects of rapamycin and 4E-BP1 on HCN4 expression.

claims.claim: Electroporated neurons in all experimental conditions showed significantly increased HCN4 staining intensity compared to the respective controls.
claims.source: Immunostaining for HCN4 channels using previously validated antibodies (Hsieh et al., 2020) in brain sections from P28-43 mice revealed significantly increased HCN4 staining intensity in the electroporated neurons in all experimental conditions compared to the respective controls, which exhibited no HCN4 staining (Figure 3a and b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 3a and b.

claims.claim: Control neurons exhibited no HCN4 staining.
claims.source: Immunostaining for HCN4 channels using previously validated antibodies (Hsieh et al., 2020) in brain sections from P28-43 mice revealed significantly increased HCN4 staining intensity in the electroporated neurons in all experimental conditions compared to the respective controls, which exhibited no HCN4 staining (Figure 3a and b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 3a and b.

claims.claim: The increased HCN4 staining was evident in the ipsilateral cortex containing MTORS2215Y electroporated neurons and absent in the non-electroporated contralateral cortex.
claims.source: The increased staining was evident in the ipsilateral cortex containing MTORS2215Y electroporated neurons and absent in the non-electroporated contralateral cortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and b.

claims.claim: RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, PtenKO, or Tsc1KO expression in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons leads to aberrant HCN4 channel expression.
claims.source: These data indicate the presence of aberrant HCN4 channel expression following RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, PtenKO, or Tsc1KO expression in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Hyperpolarizing voltage pulses elicited significantly larger inward currents in all experimental conditions compared to their respective controls.
claims.source: Consistent with previous findings in RhebS16H neurons (Hsieh et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2022), hyperpolarizing voltage pulses elicited significantly larger inward currents in all experimental conditions compared to their respective controls (Figure 3c and d, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3c and d.

claims.claim: The MTORS2215Y condition displayed larger inward currents than the RhebY35L condition.
claims.source: The MTORS2215Y condition displayed larger inward currents than the RhebY35L condition, while the PtenKO condition displayed the largest inward currents compared to the Depdc5KO and Tsc1KO conditions (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: The PtenKO condition displayed the largest inward currents compared to the Depdc5KO and Tsc1KO conditions.
claims.source: The MTORS2215Y condition displayed larger inward currents than the RhebY35L condition, while the PtenKO condition displayed the largest inward currents compared to the Depdc5KO and Tsc1KO conditions (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: The inward currents were proportional to the changes in neuron soma size.
claims.source: These data were proportional to the changes in neuron soma size (Figures 1e and 2b).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of inward current data with soma size data.

claims.claim: The ΔI-voltage (V) curve revealed significantly larger Ih amplitudes in all experimental conditions.
claims.source: The resulting ΔI-voltage (V) curve revealed significantly larger Ih amplitudes in all experimental conditions (Figure 3e, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3e.

claims.claim: At –90 mV, Ih amplitudes were significantly higher in the MTORS2215Y and Tsc1KO conditions compared to controls.
claims.source: At –90 mV, Ih amplitudes were significantly higher in the MTORS2215Y and Tsc1KO conditions compared to controls (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3f.

claims.claim: Ih currents are present in a subset of RhebY35L, Depdc5KO, and PtenKO neurons, and most MTORS2215Y and Tsc1KO neurons.
claims.source: These data suggest that Ih currents are present in a subset of RhebY35L, Depdc5KO, and PtenKO neurons, and most MTORS2215Y and Tsc1KO neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the distribution of Ih amplitudes across different conditions.

claims.claim: Application of 40 µM zatebradine reduced the overall inward currents in MTORS2215Y neurons.
claims.source: Application of 40 µM zatebradine reduced the overall inward currents (Figure 3g and h, Figure 3—source data 1) and ΔI (Figure 3i, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3g and h.

claims.claim: Application of zatebradine reduced ΔI in MTORS2215Y neurons.
claims.source: Application of 40 µM zatebradine reduced the overall inward currents (Figure 3g and h, Figure 3—source data 1) and ΔI (Figure 3i, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3i.

claims.claim: At –90 mV, ΔI was significantly decreased from –167.7 ± 54.2 pA to 0.75 ± 8.2 pA after zatebradine application.
claims.source: At –90 mV, ΔI was significantly decreased from –167.7 ± 54.2 pA to 0.75 ± 8.2 pA (± SD) (Figure 3i, arrow).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3i.

claims.claim: Zatebradine-sensitive inward currents reversed near –50 mV, as previously reported for HCN4 channel reversal potentials.
claims.source: Subtraction of the post- from the pre-zatebradine current traces isolated zatebradine-sensitive inward currents which reversed near –50 mV, as previously reported for HCN4 channel reversal potentials (Tae et al., 2017; Figure 3j and k).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3j and k and citation to Tae et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Application of the Kir channel blocker barium chloride (BaCl2) substantially reduced the overall inward currents but had no effects on ΔI (i.e. Ih) in Tsc1KO neurons.
claims.source: In comparison, application of the Kir channel blocker barium chloride (BaCl2) substantially reduced the overall inward currents but had no effects on ΔI (i.e. Ih) in Tsc1KO neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–i).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–i.

claims.claim: The application of zatebradine hyperpolarized RMP in MTORS2215Y neurons.
claims.source: Consistent with the function of Ih in maintaining RMP at depolarized levels (Lamas, 1998; Doan and Kunze, 1999; Lupica et al., 2001; Funahashi et al., 2003; Kase and Imoto, 2012), the application of zatebradine hyperpolarized RMP in MTORS2215Y neurons but did not affect the RMP of control neurons that exhibited no Ih (Figure 3l, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3l and citations to multiple studies on Ih function.

claims.claim: Zatebradine did not affect the RMP of control neurons that exhibited no Ih.
claims.source: Consistent with the function of Ih in maintaining RMP at depolarized levels (Lamas, 1998; Doan and Kunze, 1999; Lupica et al., 2001; Funahashi et al., 2003; Kase and Imoto, 2012), the application of zatebradine hyperpolarized RMP in MTORS2215Y neurons but did not affect the RMP of control neurons that exhibited no Ih (Figure 3l, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3l.

claims.claim: RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, PtenKO, and Tsc1KO expression in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons lead to the abnormal presence of HCN4 channels with variations in functional expression.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings suggest that RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, PtenKO, and Tsc1KO expression in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons lead to the abnormal presence of HCN4 channels with variations in functional expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the combined immunostaining and electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The sEPSCs frequency was unchanged in all experimental conditions except for the Tsc1KO condition, where the sEPSCs frequency was significantly increased.
claims.source: The sEPSCs frequency was unchanged in all experimental conditions except for the Tsc1KO condition, where the sEPSCs frequency was significantly increased (Figure 4a and b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4a and b.

claims.claim: The sEPSC amplitude was larger in the RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and PtenKO conditions.
claims.source: The sEPSC amplitude was larger in the RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and PtenKO conditions (Figure 4a and c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4a and c.

claims.claim: Tsc1KO neurons display increased sEPSC frequency but unchanged amplitude.
claims.source: Thus, Tsc1KO neurons display increased sEPSC frequency but unchanged amplitude, while RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and PtenKO neurons display increased sEPSC amplitude but unchanged frequency.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and PtenKO neurons display increased sEPSC amplitude but unchanged frequency.
claims.source: Thus, Tsc1KO neurons display increased sEPSC frequency but unchanged amplitude, while RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and PtenKO neurons display increased sEPSC amplitude but unchanged frequency.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: There was an increase in the sEPSC total charge in all experimental conditions except for the RhebY35L condition.
claims.source: Finally, there was an increase in the sEPSC total charge in all experimental conditions except for the RhebY35L condition (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4d.

claims.claim: All experimental conditions, except for RhebY35L, lead to increased synaptic excitability.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings suggest all experimental conditions, except for RhebY35L, lead to increased synaptic excitability, with variable impact on sEPSC frequency and amplitude.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the sEPSC data showing increased total charge in most conditions.

claims.claim: Activation of either Rheb or MTOR or biallelic inactivation Depdc5, Tsc1, or Pten largely leads to similar alterations in neuron morphology and membrane excitability but differentially impacts excitatory synaptic transmission.
claims.source: Through a combination of IUE to model the genetic mosaicism of FMCDs, histological analyses, and patch-clamp electrophysiological recordings, we found that activation of either Rheb or MTOR or biallelic inactivation Depdc5, Tsc1, or Pten, all of which increase mTORC1 activity, largely leads to similar alterations in neuron morphology and membrane excitability but differentially impacts excitatory synaptic transmission.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the combined histological and electrophysiological data presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: PtenKO neurons were correctly placed in layer 2/3, despite having one of the largest soma size increases, suggesting that cell positioning is independent of cell size.
claims.source: Interestingly, PtenKO neurons were correctly placed in layer 2/3, despite having one of the largest soma size increases, suggesting that cell positioning is independent of cell size.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PtenKO neurons have large soma size but correct positioning.

claims.claim: The lack of mispositioning of PtenKO neurons was surprising as it is thought that increased mTORC1 activity leads to neuronal misplacement.
claims.source: The lack of mispositioning of PtenKO neurons was surprising as it is thought that increased mTORC1 activity leads to neuronal misplacement, and aberrant migration of PtenKO neurons has been reported in the hippocampus (Getz et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Getz et al., 2016 and comparison with expectations based on mTORC1 activity.

claims.claim: Aberrant migration of PtenKO neurons has been reported in the hippocampus.
claims.source: The lack of mispositioning of PtenKO neurons was surprising as it is thought that increased mTORC1 activity leads to neuronal misplacement, and aberrant migration of PtenKO neurons has been reported in the hippocampus (Getz et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Getz et al., 2016.

claims.claim: PTEN has a long half-life, with a reported range of 5–20 hr or more depending on the cell type.
claims.source: Given that PTEN has a long half-life, with a reported range of 5–20 hr or more depending on the cell type (Trotman et al., 2007; Mukherjee et al., 2021; Li et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2009; Yim et al., 2009; Vazquez et al., 2000; Sacco et al., 2014), it is possible that following knockout at E15, the decreases in existing protein levels lagged behind the time window to affect neuronal migration.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on PTEN half-life.

claims.claim: TSC1 has a long half-life of ~22 hr.
claims.source: However, TSC1 also has a long half-life of ~22 hr (Lee et al., 2008; Alquezar et al., 2021), and knockout of Tsc1 at the same time point was sufficient to affect neuronal positioning.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2008 and Alquezar et al., 2021.

claims.claim: PTEN has gene-specific biological mechanisms that contribute to the lack of severe neuronal mispositioning in the developing cortex.
claims.source: Therefore, these data suggest that PTEN has gene-specific biological mechanisms that contribute to the lack of severe neuronal mispositioning in the developing cortex.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of PtenKO and Tsc1KO phenotypes despite similar protein half-lives.

claims.claim: MTORS2215Y exhibited the strongest phenotypes in terms of neuron size and positioning.
claims.source: MTORS2215Y exhibited the strongest phenotypes in terms of neuron size and positioning, which is perhaps not surprising as the mTOR protein itself forms the catalytic subunit of mTORC1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the histological data presented in Figure 1 and knowledge of mTOR's role in mTORC1.

claims.claim: Depdc5KO exhibited the mildest changes in neuron size and positioning parameters.
claims.source: Depdc5KO exhibited the mildest changes in these parameters.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the histological data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: DEPDC5 regulates mTORC1 via the GATOR1 complex in response to changes in cellular amino acid levels.
claims.source: Unlike PTEN, TSC1, RHEB, and mTOR, which regulate mTORC1 via the canonical PI3K-mTORC1 pathway in response to growth factor stimulation, DEPDC5 regulates mTORC1 via the GATOR1 complex in response to changes in cellular amino acid levels (Iffland et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Iffland et al., 2019 and established knowledge of DEPDC5 function.

claims.claim: All gene manipulations led to increased membrane conductance but decreased AP firing upon membrane depolarization.
claims.source: We found that all gene manipulations led to increased membrane conductance but decreased AP firing upon membrane depolarization, consistent with previous reports in the somatosensory cortex (Ribierre et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2015; Proietti Onori et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2018; Goz et al., 2020; Koh et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022) and in the mPFC for the RhebS16H condition (Hsieh et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2 and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Inhibiting firing in cortical pyramidal neurons expressing the RhebS16H mutation via co-expression of Kir2.1 channels prevents seizures.
claims.source: However, inhibiting firing in cortical pyramidal neurons expressing the RhebS16H mutation via co-expression of Kir2.1 channels (to hyperpolarize neurons and shunt their firing) has been shown to prevent seizures, supporting a cell-autonomous mechanism (Hsieh et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hsieh et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The abnormal expression of HCN4 channels in the RhebS16H neurons was found to be mTORC1-dependent by their sensitivity to rapamycin and the expression of constitutive active 4E-BP1.
claims.source: The abnormal expression of HCN4 channels in the RhebS16H neurons was found to be mTORC1-dependent by their sensitivity to rapamycin and the expression of constitutive active 4E-BP1.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on previous experimental findings regarding HCN4 channel expression.

claims.claim: The abnormal HCN4 channel expression has been verified in resected human FCDII and HME tissue (of unknown genetic etiology).
claims.source: In addition, the abnormal HCN4 channel expression has been verified in resected human FCDII and HME tissue (of unknown genetic etiology) (Hsieh et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hsieh et al., 2020 and Nguyen et al., 2022.

claims.claim: RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, PtenKO, and Tsc1KO cortical neurons display aberrant HCN4 channel expression, which is consistent with the mTORC1-dependent mode of expression in RhebS16H neurons.
claims.source: Here, we found that RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, PtenKO, and Tsc1KO cortical neurons also display aberrant HCN4 channel expression, which is consistent with the mTORC1-dependent mode of expression in RhebS16H neurons (Hsieh et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the HCN4 immunostaining and electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3 and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Increased Kir channels contribute to the enlarged inward currents in all the conditions investigated.
claims.source: In addition to HCN4 channels, it is thought that increased Kir channels, which are well-known to hyperpolarize RMPs, contribute to the enlarged inward currents in all the conditions we investigated.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the electrophysiological data and knowledge of Kir channel function.

claims.claim: Application of BaCl2 to block Kir channels reduced the overall inward current and depolarized RMPs in Tsc1KO neurons.
claims.source: This was confirmed in the Tsc1KO neurons where the application of BaCl2 to block Kir channels reduced the overall inward current and depolarized RMPs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Abnormal HCN4 channel expression is a conserved mechanism across mTORC1-activating gene conditions.
claims.source: Nevertheless, our data suggests that abnormal HCN4 channel expression is a conserved mechanism across these mTORC1-activating gene conditions and warrants further investigation of HCN-mediated excitability in mTORC1-related epilepsy.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of HCN4 expression across all gene conditions tested.

claims.claim: Increased sEPSC frequency with no sEPSC amplitude changes in layer 2/3 cortical pyramidal neurons from 4-week-old Tsc1 conditional KO mice has been previously reported.
claims.source: This finding corroborates a previous study showing increased sEPSC frequency with no sEPSC amplitude changes in layer 2/3 cortical pyramidal neurons from 4-week-old Tsc1 conditional KO mice (Wu et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The sEPSC frequency in RhebS16H neurons was reduced by 25%.
claims.source: Interestingly, as previously reported for RhebS16H neurons (Lin et al., 2016), the sEPSC frequency in RhebY35L neurons was reduced by 25% but this did not reach statistical significance, possibly due to a generally weaker effect of the Y35L mutation compared to the S16H mutation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2016 and comparison with current data.

claims.claim: Despite impinging on mTORC1 signaling, different mTORC1 pathway gene mutations can affect synaptic activity, and thereby, excitability differently.
claims.source: Thus, despite impinging on mTORC1 signaling, different mTORC1 pathway gene mutations can affect synaptic activity, and thereby, excitability differently.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects on sEPSC properties across gene conditions.

claims.claim: Loss of PTEN increases mTORC2 activity.
claims.source: Loss of PTEN increases mTORC2 activity, whereas loss of TSC1/2 and DEPDC5 is associated with decreased mTORC2 activity (Zhou et al., 2009; Nguyen et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2008; Yuskaitis et al., 2018; Karalis et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on mTORC2 activity.

claims.claim: Loss of TSC1/2 and DEPDC5 is associated with decreased mTORC2 activity.
claims.source: Loss of PTEN increases mTORC2 activity, whereas loss of TSC1/2 and DEPDC5 is associated with decreased mTORC2 activity (Zhou et al., 2009; Nguyen et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2008; Yuskaitis et al., 2018; Karalis et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on mTORC2 activity.

claims.claim: Inhibition of mTORC2 reduces neuronal overgrowth but not the synaptic defects and seizures associated with PTEN loss.
claims.source: Studies have shown that inhibition of mTORC2 reduces neuronal overgrowth but not the synaptic defects and seizures associated with PTEN loss (Cullen et al., 2023; Cullen et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cullen et al., 2023 and Cullen et al., 2024.

claims.claim: Inhibition of mTORC2 reduces seizures in several epilepsy models, including the MTORS2215F gain-of-function and Pten KO models.
claims.source: However, other studies have reported that inhibition of mTORC2 reduces seizures in several epilepsy models, including the MTORS2215F gain-of-function and Pten KO models (Chen et al., 2019; Okoh et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2019 and Okoh et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Human cytomegalic neurons have increased capacitance and decreased input resistance.
claims.source: These studies showed that human cytomegalic neurons have increased capacitance and decreased input resistance (Cepeda et al., 2003; Cepeda et al., 2005), consistent with our findings in the present and previous studies in mice (Hsieh et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cepeda et al., 2003 and Cepeda et al., 2005.

claims.claim: The frequency of sEPSC was higher in neurons in TSC compared to FCDII in human tissue.
claims.source: In particular, the frequency of sEPSC was higher in neurons in TSC compared to FCDII.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of human electrophysiology data from TSC and FCDII cases.

claims.claim: Although TSC and FCDII share several histopathologic similarities, there are subtle functional differences between these disorders.
claims.source: The authors of the 2010 human electrophysiology study concluded that although TSC and FCDII share several histopathologic similarities, there are subtle functional differences between these disorders (Cepeda et al., 2010), aligning with the overall conclusions from our study.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cepeda et al., 2010.

claims.claim: A functional reduction of GABAA-mediated synaptic transmission in cortical pyramidal neurons in individuals with FCDII has been reported.
claims.source: Another study has reported a functional reduction of GABAA-mediated synaptic transmission in cortical pyramidal neurons in individuals with FCDII (Calcagnotto et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Calcagnotto et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Brain somatic mutations causing FMCDs occur throughout cortical neurogenesis in neural progenitor cells that give rise to excitatory (pyramidal) neurons.
claims.source: Brain somatic mutations causing FMCDs, such as FCDII and HME, occur throughout cortical neurogenesis in neural progenitor cells that give rise to excitatory (pyramidal) neurons (D'Gama et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to D'Gama et al., 2017 and Chung et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Mutations affecting different mTORC1 pathway genes have similar and dissimilar consequences on cortical pyramidal neuron development and function.
claims.source: In summary, we have shown that mutations affecting different mTORC1 pathway genes have similar and dissimilar consequences on cortical pyramidal neuron development and function, which may affect how neurons behave in cortical circuits.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Cortical neurons harboring different mTORC1 pathway gene mutations may differentially affect how neurons receive and process cortical inputs.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that cortical neurons harboring different mTORC1 pathway gene mutations may differentially affect how neurons receive and process cortical inputs, which have implications for the mechanisms of cortical hyperexcitability and seizures in FMCDs, and potentially affect how neurons and their networks respond to therapeutic intervention.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects on synaptic properties across gene conditions.

results.result: Expression of RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, PtenKO, and Tsc1KO all led to increased mTORC1 signaling (measured by p-S6 staining) and increased neuron soma size, with gene-specific magnitudes of enlargement. MTORS2215Y and RhebY35L showed the largest increases (>3-fold), PtenKO showed 2.7-fold increase, Tsc1KO showed 2.1-fold increase, and Depdc5KO showed the smallest increase (1.7-fold).
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C26 are well-supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1c-d) showing increased p-S6 levels and quantitative morphometric analysis (Figure 1e) demonstrating statistically significant, gene-specific increases in soma size. The data include appropriate sample sizes (4-8 mice per group, 6-15 cells per animal) and statistical analyses (nested one-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests).

results.result: All experimental conditions except PtenKO resulted in neuron mispositioning, with RhebY35L and MTORS2215Y showing the most severe phenotype (~70-80% misplaced), Depdc5KO and Tsc1KO showing intermediate phenotypes (~45-60% misplaced), and PtenKO neurons remaining correctly positioned in layer 2/3 despite large soma size. This suggests that neuronal positioning defects occur independently of cell size.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C31 and C82 are supported by quantitative positioning data (Figure 1f-h) showing statistically significant differences in neuron placement across conditions. The observation that PtenKO neurons have large soma size but correct positioning provides strong evidence for the independence of these phenotypes. Sample sizes (3-7 mice per group) and statistical methods (one-way ANOVA, two-way repeated measures ANOVA) are appropriate.

results.result: All experimental conditions showed increased membrane capacitance and resting membrane conductance, with gene-specific magnitudes. MTORS2215Y neurons had larger capacitance increases than RhebY35L, while PtenKO and Tsc1KO had similar increases that were both larger than Depdc5KO.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 2b-c) from 5-10 mice per group with 16-50 cells analyzed per animal. The data show statistically significant increases in capacitance and conductance across all conditions, with appropriate statistical analyses (nested one-way ANOVA). The findings are consistent with the observed increases in soma size.

results.result: RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and Tsc1KO expression led to depolarized resting membrane potential (RMP), while Depdc5KO and PtenKO expression did not significantly affect RMP. Despite depolarized RMPs, RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and Tsc1KO neurons showed decreased ability to generate action potentials upon depolarization.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C37, and C41 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 2d) showing gene-specific effects on RMP. The paradoxical finding of depolarized RMP with decreased excitability is well-documented with appropriate sample sizes and statistical analyses. The inference in C41 is reasonable given the combined observations of RMP and rheobase data.

results.result: All experimental conditions led to decreased depolarization-induced excitability, as evidenced by fewer action potentials fired in response to current injections above 100 pA and increased rheobase. MTORS2215Y and RhebY35L conditions showed the largest rheobase increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 and C49 are supported by comprehensive electrophysiological data (Figure 2e-g) showing statistically significant decreases in AP firing and increases in rheobase across all conditions. The data include appropriate sample sizes, controls, and statistical analyses (nested one-way ANOVA, mixed-effects ANOVA). This represents a convergent phenotype across different mTORC1 pathway mutations.

results.result: Control neurons displayed an initial spike doublet consistent with layer 2/3 mPFC pyramidal neurons, which was absent in all experimental conditions except PtenKO. RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, and Tsc1KO neurons showed significantly increased first interspike interval (ISI), while PtenKO neurons did not.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 2e, 2h) showing altered firing patterns. The presence of spike doublets in controls is validated by citation to Kroon et al., 2019. The quantitative ISI data show statistically significant increases in most conditions except PtenKO, with appropriate statistical analyses.

results.result: No differences in AP threshold were observed across conditions. AP peak amplitude was decreased in MTORS2215Y and Tsc1KO conditions, while AP half-width was decreased in RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and PtenKO conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 2i-k) showing gene-specific effects on AP properties. The data include appropriate sample sizes and statistical analyses. These findings represent gene-specific differences in action potential kinetics.

results.result: All experimental conditions (RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, PtenKO, Tsc1KO) showed significantly increased HCN4 channel expression compared to controls, which exhibited no HCN4 staining. The increased HCN4 staining was specific to electroporated neurons in the ipsilateral cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 and C74 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 3a-b) using previously validated antibodies. The data show statistically significant increases in HCN4 staining intensity across all conditions (4-8 mice per group, 4-15 cells per animal). The specificity is confirmed by ipsilateral vs. contralateral comparisons and no-primary antibody controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

results.result: Hyperpolarizing voltage pulses elicited significantly larger inward currents and Ih amplitudes in all experimental conditions compared to controls. MTORS2215Y showed larger currents than RhebY35L, and PtenKO showed the largest currents compared to Depdc5KO and Tsc1KO. At -90 mV, Ih amplitudes were significantly higher in MTORS2215Y and Tsc1KO conditions. Ih currents were present in a subset of RhebY35L, Depdc5KO, and PtenKO neurons, and most MTORS2215Y and Tsc1KO neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66 are supported by voltage-clamp recordings (Figure 3c-f) with appropriate sample sizes (5-10 mice per group, 24-47 cells per animal). The data show statistically significant increases in inward currents and Ih amplitudes, with gene-specific magnitudes. The inference in C63 about proportionality to soma size is reasonable. The conclusion in C66 about subset expression is appropriately cautious given the variability in some conditions.

results.result: Application of the HCN channel blocker zatebradine (40 µM) to MTORS2215Y neurons reduced overall inward currents and ΔI, with ΔI at -90 mV decreasing from -167.7 ± 54.2 pA to 0.75 ± 8.2 pA. Zatebradine-sensitive currents reversed near -50 mV, consistent with HCN4 channel reversal potentials. Zatebradine hyperpolarized RMP in MTORS2215Y neurons but not in control neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70, C72-C73 are supported by pharmacological experiments (Figure 3g-l) showing specific blockade of Ih by zatebradine. The reversal potential near -50 mV is consistent with published HCN4 channel properties (cited: Tae et al., 2017). The effect on RMP is consistent with Ih function in maintaining depolarized RMP (multiple citations provided). Sample sizes are adequate (4-6 neurons, paired measurements).

results.result: Application of the Kir channel blocker BaCl2 (200 µM) substantially reduced overall inward currents and depolarized RMP in Tsc1KO neurons but had no effects on ΔI (Ih).
results.evaluation: Claims C71 and C97 are supported by pharmacological experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showing that BaCl2 blocks Kir channels but not Ih. This provides important control data distinguishing Kir-mediated currents from HCN-mediated currents. Sample sizes are adequate (10-13 neurons per group) with appropriate statistical analyses.

results.result: sEPSC frequency was unchanged in all conditions except Tsc1KO (significantly increased). sEPSC amplitude was larger in RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and PtenKO conditions. sEPSC total charge was increased in all conditions except RhebY35L. These findings suggest that all experimental conditions except RhebY35L lead to increased synaptic excitability, with variable impacts on frequency and amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 are supported by spontaneous EPSC recordings (Figure 4) with appropriate sample sizes (5-9 mice per group, 17-34 cells per animal). The data show gene-specific effects on synaptic transmission with statistically significant differences. The inference in C80 about increased synaptic excitability is reasonable based on the total charge data, though the RhebY35L exception is notable.

results.result: Activation of Rheb or MTOR or biallelic inactivation of Depdc5, Tsc1, or Pten largely leads to similar alterations in neuron morphology and membrane excitability but differentially impacts excitatory synaptic transmission. These findings suggest that cortical neurons harboring different mTORC1 pathway gene mutations may differentially affect how neurons receive and process cortical inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C81, C111, and C112 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing data from all experimental approaches. The claims are well-supported by the comprehensive histological, electrophysiological, and synaptic data presented throughout the manuscript. The conclusion about convergent morphological/membrane phenotypes and divergent synaptic phenotypes is justified by the data, though the mechanistic implications remain somewhat speculative.

results.result: The lack of mispositioning of PtenKO neurons was surprising given that increased mTORC1 activity is thought to lead to neuronal misplacement, and aberrant migration of PtenKO neurons has been reported in hippocampus. Despite both PTEN and TSC1 having long half-lives (5-20 hr for PTEN, ~22 hr for TSC1), only Tsc1KO affected neuronal positioning, suggesting PTEN has gene-specific biological mechanisms that contribute to the lack of severe neuronal mispositioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 present a discussion of the unexpected PtenKO positioning phenotype. While the observation is well-documented (C30, C82), the mechanistic explanation based on protein half-life (C85-C86) is speculative. The inference in C87 about gene-specific mechanisms is reasonable but not directly tested. The comparison to hippocampal data (C84) is appropriately cited but may not be directly applicable to cortical migration.

results.result: MTORS2215Y exhibited the strongest phenotypes in neuron size and positioning, which is consistent with mTOR forming the catalytic subunit of mTORC1. Depdc5KO exhibited the mildest changes. Unlike other genes that regulate mTORC1 via the canonical PI3K-mTORC1 pathway, DEPDC5 regulates mTORC1 via the GATOR1 complex in response to amino acid levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by the histological data (Figure 1) and established knowledge of mTORC1 pathway organization. The observation about MTORS2215Y severity is well-documented. The explanation for Depdc5KO mildness based on different regulatory mechanisms (C90) is supported by citation to Iffland et al., 2019 and represents reasonable interpretation.

results.result: Previous work showed that RhebS16H neurons display abnormal HCN4 channel expression that gives rise to Ih normally absent in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons. This aberrant Ih preceded seizure onset (detected by P8-12) and was prevented/alleviated by rapamycin and constitutive active 4E-BP1, indicating mTORC1-dependence. The current study extends these findings to show that RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, PtenKO, and Tsc1KO also display aberrant HCN4 expression, suggesting this is a conserved mechanism across mTORC1-activating gene conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C55, C93-C95, and C98 appropriately cite prior work (Hsieh et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2022) and extend those findings to additional gene conditions. The current data (Figure 3) support the extension to new gene conditions. However, the claim of mTORC1-dependence for the new conditions (C95, C98) is inferred from prior work rather than directly tested with rapamycin in each condition, which represents a limitation.

results.result: All gene manipulations led to increased membrane conductance but decreased AP firing upon membrane depolarization, consistent with previous reports. However, inhibiting firing in RhebS16H neurons via Kir2.1 channel co-expression prevents seizures, supporting a cell-autonomous mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 are supported by the current electrophysiological data (Figure 2) and appropriately cite previous studies showing similar findings in other cortical regions and the RhebS16H condition. The citation to Hsieh et al., 2020 regarding seizure prevention by Kir2.1 is appropriate and helps reconcile the apparent paradox of decreased intrinsic excitability in epilepsy models.

results.result: In addition to HCN4 channels, increased Kir channels contribute to the enlarged inward currents in all conditions investigated.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is based on inference from electrophysiological data and knowledge of Kir channel function, but is only directly tested in Tsc1KO neurons (C97, Figure 3—figure supplement 3). While the inference is reasonable given the large inward currents at hyperpolarized potentials, the claim that this applies to "all conditions" is not fully supported by direct experimental evidence in each condition.

results.result: The finding of increased sEPSC frequency in Tsc1KO neurons corroborates a previous study in Tsc1 conditional KO mice. The sEPSC frequency in RhebY35L neurons was reduced by 25% (not statistically significant), similar to previous reports for RhebS16H neurons. These findings suggest that different mTORC1 pathway gene mutations can affect synaptic activity differently.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 appropriately cite previous work (Wu et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2016) and compare current findings to published data. The observation of gene-specific effects on synaptic activity is well-supported by the data (Figure 4). The inference in C101 about differential effects is reasonable and represents a key conclusion of the study.

results.result: Loss of PTEN increases mTORC2 activity, whereas loss of TSC1/2 and DEPDC5 is associated with decreased mTORC2 activity. Studies show conflicting results regarding whether mTORC2 inhibition reduces seizures, with some showing reduction of neuronal overgrowth but not synaptic defects/seizures in PTEN loss models, while others report seizure reduction in MTORS2215F and Pten KO models.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 appropriately cite multiple studies on mTORC2 activity and its role in epilepsy. The claims accurately represent the conflicting findings in the literature regarding mTORC2's contribution to seizures. However, these claims are entirely based on prior work and do not represent new findings from the current study. The discussion appropriately acknowledges the uncertainty in this area.

results.result: Human electrophysiology studies showed that cytomegalic neurons have increased capacitance and decreased input resistance, consistent with current findings in mice. Comparisons between TSC and FCDII cases showed similar passive membrane properties but differences in sEPSC frequency (higher in TSC), with authors concluding there are subtle functional differences between these disorders. A functional reduction of GABAA-mediated synaptic transmission in FCDII has also been reported.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C109 appropriately cite human electrophysiology studies (Cepeda et al., 2003, 2005, 2010; Calcagnotto et al., 2005) and compare findings to the current mouse data. The citations appear accurate and the comparisons are reasonable. However, the genetic etiology of the human FCDII cases is unknown, limiting direct comparison to the gene-specific mouse models. The discussion appropriately acknowledges this limitation.

results.result: Background claims establishing that brain somatic mutations in mTORC1 pathway components are major causes of focal malformations of cortical development (FMCDs) and intractable epilepsy, describing the mTORC1 pathway organization and regulation, and noting that these mutations occur in neural progenitor cells during fetal development resulting in brain somatic mosaicism.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C4-C19, and C110 represent background information appropriately supported by citations to established literature. These claims accurately describe the current understanding of mTORopathies, the mTORC1 signaling pathway, and the genetic basis of FMCDs. The citations appear appropriate and the claims represent accurate summaries of prior work.

results.result: The main findings of the study: in utero activation of Rheb or MTOR or biallelic inactivation of Depdc5, Tsc1, or Pten leads to shared alterations in pyramidal neuron morphology, positioning, and membrane excitability but different changes in excitatory synaptic transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C3 represent the main findings stated in the abstract and are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including histological analyses (Figure 1), electrophysiological recordings (Figures 2-3), and synaptic measurements (Figure 4). These claims accurately summarize the key results of the study.

results.result: All five mTORC1 pathway gene manipulations (RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, PtenKO, and Tsc1KO) led to increased mTORC1 signaling as measured by p-S6 staining, and resulted in enlarged neuron soma size, with MTORS2215Y and RhebY35L showing the largest increases (>3-fold), PtenKO showing 2.7-fold increase, and Depdc5KO showing the mildest increase (1.7-fold).
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. Reviewer 1 states the evidence is 'compelling' and demonstrates 'convergent mTOR pathway activation and alterations of neuronal morphology.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the investigators demonstrate that gene KO or activation leads to common changes in cell size (enlargement)' and confirms 'Expression of the RhebY35L, mTORS2215Y, Dedpdc5KO, PtenKO, and Tsc1KO plasmids all led to significantly increased p-S6 staining intensity.'

results.result: Four of the five gene manipulations (RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, and Tsc1KO) caused neuron mispositioning outside layer 2/3, with RhebY35L and MTORS2215Y showing the most severe phenotype (70-80% misplaced). Notably, PtenKO neurons remained correctly positioned in layer 2/3 despite having large soma size (2.7-fold increase), suggesting that cell positioning is independent of cell size and that PTEN has gene-specific mechanisms affecting migration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly highlights this as a key finding, stating 'while RhebY35L, mTORS2215Y, Dedpdc5KO, and Tsc1KO significantly disrupted laminar positioning of neurons in layer 2/3, PtenKO had minimal effects on laminar positioning. This finding is intriguing since it means that simply activating mTOR during fetal brain development will not necessarily alter cortical lamination and that an increase in cell size by itself doesn't disrupt laminar fidelity.' The editor notes this demonstrates 'gene-specific mechanisms.'

results.result: All five gene manipulations led to increased membrane capacitance and conductance, and universally decreased depolarization-induced excitability (fewer action potentials and increased rheobase). However, only RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and Tsc1KO caused depolarized resting membrane potentials, while Depdc5KO and PtenKO did not significantly affect RMP, demonstrating gene-dependent differences in membrane properties.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly confirms these findings: 'Expression of RhebY35L, mTORS2215Y, Dedpdc5KO, PtenKO, and Tsc1KO led to decreased depolarization-induced excitability, but only RhebY35L, mTORS2215Y, and Tsc1KO expression led to depolarized resting membrane potentials.' Reviewer 1 notes the study demonstrates 'differential impact on excitatory synaptic activity' and the editor emphasizes 'gene-specific mechanisms of hyperexcitability.'

results.result: The characteristic spike doublet firing pattern of layer 2/3 mPFC pyramidal neurons was absent in RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, Depdc5KO, and Tsc1KO conditions but preserved in PtenKO neurons. This was reflected in significantly increased first interspike intervals in all conditions except PtenKO. Additional gene-specific differences were observed in action potential properties including peak amplitude and half-width.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges these findings as part of the comprehensive electrophysiological characterization, noting that the study shows 'gene-dependent changes in RMP and several AP properties.' The preservation of normal firing patterns in PtenKO neurons aligns with the reviewers' emphasis on gene-specific differences despite common mTOR activation.

results.result: All five gene manipulations led to aberrant HCN4 channel expression in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons (where HCN4 is normally absent), with corresponding increases in hyperpolarization-activated inward currents (Ih). The magnitude of Ih varied across conditions, with MTORS2215Y and Tsc1KO showing the most robust functional expression, suggesting HCN4 channel expression is a conserved mTORC1-dependent mechanism across different mTORC1 pathway gene mutations.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states: 'Interestingly, expression of RhebY35L, mTORS2215Y, Dedpdc5KO, PtenKO, and Tsc1KO led to the abnormal presence of HCN4 channels with variations in functional expression suggesting a common cellular mechanism that could confer excitability.' Reviewer 1 notes this as providing 'novel insights into the mechanism of seizure generation.' The reviewers treat this as a significant shared mechanism despite variations in magnitude.

results.result: Application of the HCN channel blocker zatebradine to MTORS2215Y neurons reduced inward currents and hyperpolarized the resting membrane potential, confirming the functional identity of the aberrant currents as Ih mediated by HCN4 channels. The zatebradine-sensitive currents reversed near -50 mV, consistent with HCN4 channel properties.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly confirms this validation: 'Effects of treatment with the selective HCN channel blocker zatebradine on hyperpolarization-induced inward currents in mTORS2215Y neurons confirmed the identity of ΔI as Ih.' This pharmacological validation strengthens the claim that the observed currents are indeed HCN4-mediated.

results.result: In addition to HCN4 channels, increased Kir channels contribute to the enlarged inward currents in mTORC1-activated neurons. Application of the Kir channel blocker BaCl2 to Tsc1KO neurons reduced overall inward currents and depolarized resting membrane potentials, but did not affect Ih (ΔI), confirming the distinct contributions of Kir and HCN4 channels.
results.evaluation: While not explicitly discussed by reviewers, this finding is presented as supporting data that distinguishes between Kir and HCN4 channel contributions. The reviewers' acceptance of the overall HCN4 findings and lack of critique of the Kir channel data suggests implicit acceptance of this supporting mechanistic detail.

results.result: Different mTORC1 pathway gene mutations had distinct effects on excitatory synaptic transmission: Tsc1KO neurons showed increased sEPSC frequency but unchanged amplitude, while RhebY35L, MTORS2215Y, and PtenKO neurons showed increased sEPSC amplitude but unchanged frequency. Most conditions (except RhebY35L) showed increased sEPSC total charge, indicating increased synaptic excitability through different mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly emphasizes this as a key finding, stating the study demonstrates 'differential impact on excitatory synaptic activity, conferring gene-specific mechanisms of hyperexcitability.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Expression of RhebY35L, mTORS2215Y, Dedpdc5KO, PtenKO, and Tsc1KO led to different impacts on sEPSC properties.' The editor highlights this as demonstrating 'different changes in excitatory synaptic transmission.'

results.result: The study's central finding is that while in utero activation or inactivation of different mTORC1 pathway genes leads to shared alterations in pyramidal neuron morphology, positioning, and membrane excitability, these mutations differentially impact excitatory synaptic transmission. This suggests that cortical neurons harboring different mTORC1 pathway gene mutations may differentially affect how neurons receive and process cortical inputs, with implications for seizure mechanisms and therapeutic responses.
results.evaluation: All reviewers strongly support this overarching conclusion. The editor states the manuscript 'bridges several different genetic causes of focal malformations' and the evidence is 'compelling.' Reviewer 1 notes the findings 'provide novel insights into the mechanism of seizure generation.' Reviewer 3 states 'The study clearly achieves its stated aims' and provides 'convincing and compelling direct comparison' showing both 'common changes' and 'distinct genetic effects despite a common effect on mTOR signaling.'

results.result: Among the gene manipulations, MTORS2215Y exhibited the strongest phenotypes in neuron size and positioning (consistent with mTOR being the catalytic subunit of mTORC1), while Depdc5KO showed the mildest changes. This difference may relate to DEPDC5 regulating mTORC1 via the GATOR1 complex in response to amino acid levels, rather than through the canonical PI3K-mTORC1 pathway.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'The major effect was seen in forebrain neurons expressing mTORS2215Y' and acknowledges the gene-specific differences. While one reviewer mentions that 'consideration of distinct metabolic states i.e., amino acid levels would have strengthened the study,' this is presented as a suggestion for future work rather than a critique of the current findings.

results.result: The manuscript discusses that loss of PTEN increases mTORC2 activity while loss of TSC1/2 and DEPDC5 decreases mTORC2 activity, and that studies show conflicting results regarding whether mTORC2 inhibition reduces seizures in different epilepsy models, suggesting complex interactions between mTORC1 and mTORC2 pathways.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes that 'analysis of the role of the mTORC2 pathway...would have strengthened the study,' indicating this is an area where additional investigation would be valuable. The reviewers do not challenge the cited literature on mTORC2, but the suggestion for additional analysis implies the current treatment of mTORC2's role is incomplete rather than fully resolved.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C20-C26 regarding mTORC1 activation and soma enlargement. Both evaluations find the immunostaining and morphometric data compelling and well-supported with appropriate statistical analyses.

Strong agreement on claims C27-C31, C82 regarding neuronal positioning. Both highlight the key finding that PtenKO neurons show correct positioning despite enlarged soma size, demonstrating gene-specific mechanisms. Peer review explicitly emphasizes this as an intriguing finding showing that mTOR activation alone doesn't necessarily disrupt lamination.

Agreement on claims C32-C35 regarding capacitance and conductance increases. Peer review R3 encompasses broader electrophysiological findings (C32-C41, C49, C91) while OpenEval R3 focuses specifically on membrane properties. Both find the data well-supported.

Overlap on claims C36-C37, C41 regarding RMP changes. OpenEval R4 focuses on gene-specific RMP effects, while peer R3 covers broader electrophysiological phenotypes including decreased excitability. Both support the findings with appropriate acknowledgment of gene-specific differences.

Overlap on claims C38-C40, C49 regarding decreased AP firing and increased rheobase. OpenEval R5 emphasizes this as a convergent phenotype across conditions, while peer R3 integrates this with other electrophysiological findings. Both evaluations support the data.

Agreement on claims C42-C45 regarding altered firing patterns and spike doublets. OpenEval R6 provides detailed analysis of ISI data, while peer R4 acknowledges these as part of comprehensive gene-dependent changes in action potential properties. Both find the evidence supported.

Overlap on claims C46-C48 regarding gene-specific AP properties. OpenEval R7 focuses on AP kinetics, while peer R4 groups these with broader firing pattern changes. Both evaluations support the findings as demonstrating gene-specific differences.

Agreement on claims C56-C59, C74 regarding HCN4 upregulation. OpenEval R8 emphasizes the immunostaining validation and controls, while peer R5 highlights this as a common cellular mechanism across conditions with variations in magnitude. Both find the evidence compelling.

Agreement on claims C60-C66 regarding Ih currents and functional HCN4 expression. OpenEval R9 details the voltage-clamp data and gene-specific magnitudes, while peer R5 emphasizes this as a novel shared mechanism conferring excitability. Both support the findings with acknowledgment of variability.

Perfect agreement on claims C67-C70, C72-C73 regarding zatebradine blockade of Ih and HCN4 validation. Both evaluations confirm the pharmacological evidence supports HCN4 channel identity and its role in maintaining depolarized RMP.

Agreement on claims C71, C97 regarding BaCl2 blockade distinguishing Kir from HCN channels. OpenEval R11 explicitly discusses this control data, while peer R7 implicitly accepts it as supporting mechanistic detail without critique.

Strong agreement on claims C75-C80 regarding gene-specific synaptic transmission effects. OpenEval R12 details the sEPSC data, while peer R8 emphasizes this as a key finding demonstrating differential impact on excitatory synaptic activity and gene-specific mechanisms of hyperexcitability.

Strong agreement on claims C81, C111-C112 representing main conclusions. Both evaluations find the synthesis of convergent morphological/membrane phenotypes and divergent synaptic phenotypes well-supported. Peer review emphasizes the study achieves its aims with compelling evidence bridging different genetic causes.

Partial overlap on claims C83, C87 regarding PtenKO positioning mechanisms.
